issue_context.title: [Feature] Add annotations for test.step similar to test
issue_context.body:
Currently skip option is available on test case level(https://playwright.dev/docs/test-annotations)

But there is no skip /similar annotations in test step level

**Expected**

test.step.skip
test.step.only
test.step.fail (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/10033)
comments: I have a situation where one test step works on chromium and firefox but fails on WebKit due to the latest trunk build for the playwright WebKit browser.  I would like to skip the test step just for WebKit and only that step since the other ones work fine for all of the browsers.  Having annotations added to the test.step() level and not just the parent level test() method would substantially help to organize and provide correct results for reporting without having to add if/else conditionals all over the test file.

test.step.skip in reports:
```
Total steps: x
Skipped: y
```
❤️

> Sometimes there may be a reason to skip a step, especially if that step is just for checking content, i.e. test.expect
> 
> For example
> 
> ```
> test("update profile", async function () {
> 	test.step("update");
> 	test.step.skip("check part A"); // part A currently disabled due to frontend bugs
> 	test.step("check part B");
> })
> ```
> 
> it's better than commenting out the step

Totally agree
Adding my vote!  I just went to skip a new test step and discovered that there was no such option.  I just expected it would be there, its intuitive that it would exist.
This is definitely a valuable feature. My use case is for a step that does not work across all test environments at the moment so need to skip it to avoid unnecessary test failures.

I have been recently working to improve our end-to-end tests at my company, and a lot of good work's been done. Only thing I am missing is having the ability to just `test.step.skip` instead of commenting it out.

I reckon there has to be a temporary way to be able to implement it ourselves, till Playwright officially adds it. I am not looking for being able to pass a condition into test.step like we have for test.

Just adding a `.skip` should skip that step without supplying a condition.

Another use case: We use skipped tests in our daily smoke testing reporting to see which tests we know are currently disabled (because they found a bug that is currently being worked on, and we disable the tests to not have red pipelines all the times, until the bug is fixed).

It would be super helpful to only disable some steps of a test that perform the checks for the things that are currently broken, have the rest of the test still being executed, and getting this "test X step Y was skipped" message in the reports
+1 For this request, would be super useful.

+1 very handy ask, I do not want to skip the entire test just skip the test.step that is looking for a specific context in the whole test aka, a button can have 4 different classes, I'd like to test.step each class scenario but skip it if on an entire grid of which there are many assigned classes, if 1/4 classes are not present, skip the test.step targeting them. it would be handy
This would be super helpful so voting this to get added as well.
another +1, would be really helpful
another +1, would be really helpful if we can skip a test with or without condition
+1 this is needed.
Please, lets just add 👍 reaction to the first message.

> Could you help me understand why the following notation is not solving this request?

That approach is viable and something I've personally used but I do think a dedicated method does provide a bit cleaner syntax. I wonder what the motivations for `test.skip` originally were, I am sure there would be some crossover here.

On another note, that kind of conditional logic is also seemingly against [recommend best practices](https://github.com/playwright-community/eslint-plugin-playwright/blob/main/docs/rules/no-conditional-in-test.md) and flags warnings for me. However I am aware that's a bit of a "six of one, half a dozen of the other" scenario.

@quoid 

> I wonder what the motivations for `test.skip` originally were

Just like `test.skip` gives finer control over which tests execute based on certain conditions that can be evaluated at runtime. In the same way, `step.skip` will give finer control over which steps contribute towards the test based on some conditions that can be evaluated at runtime.

There are times where one may want to skip a step from executing when run in a different (but similar) environment. Some steps may not be applicable or become additional steps depending upon the execution environment. I would not want to maintain two copies of similar test with minor differences.
This would be really good added benefit. I don't want to skip a whole test because one or two steps need to be skipped, especially when the rest of the test runs just fine.

We have `skipIf` and `runIf` on `describe` & `test/it` statements also supporting async conditions in something like `vitest` and it works quite well. Does it make sense to 'standardise' this behaviour?

I think the `fail` annotation is equally as important as the other ones.
I created a separate issue because it looks like nobody is talking about this here.

I do support the idea of adding this functionality, specially because it will give certainty by providing visibility in reports, also I do second the comment from @quoid that having this will provide a clearer and standardized way to write better tests cases.

Our team is currently wrapping the whole step with a comment along with a TODO statement as a reminder for us to work on it in the future; this is only visible if you are reading the code but not visible in the reports, which would be very nice to have. Same case if you add a condition, this will be visible in code but not in the reports.

To have it in the reports, the only workaround is to change `step` to `test`, and then wrap all the `test` with a `describe`, but this will inject more constrains since `test` are a different thing, so no way to achieve it.
3 years and something that would be incredibly simple to code and be of great value to everyone is still not done. :(
Seriously this needs to be picked up its so simple and people need it

> Seriously this needs to be picked up its so simple and people need it

"so simple" then submit a PR...

> "so simple" then submit a PR...

You know full well that it would be simple for those familiar with the codebase. For those who aren't it's a whole different ball game.

Then there's the potential hassle of trying to contribute to repos that are heavily gate kept. A quick look at the PR's for a repo usually answers that question.

Hi @yury-s 

I see there is `test.step.fixme()` added, but no `test.step.skip()`. Is it intentional?

> I see there is `test.step.fixme()` added, but no `test.step.skip()`. Is it intentional?

To me it looks like fixme would cover the requested skip for many developers.

> To me it looks like fixme would cover the requested skip for many developers.

I'm thinking about API consistency. For `test` there are both `.skip()` and `.fixme()`, but for `test.step` there is only `.fixme()`. I guess many developers will habitually write `test.step.skip` and get `undefined is not a function`.
More predictable API is better DX.

Agree with @vitalets, especially considering the OP indicates a completely different API proposal from the closing commit referencing this issue. https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/pull/34042 says it fixes/closes this issue but only includes `fail` and `fixme` whereas this issue proposes `skip`, `only`, and `fail`

Agree with the other comments here. Don't understand why `skip` and `only` were disregarded when they are in the original proposal.

Marking a skipped test step as `fixme` or `fail` is contextually very different to `skip` and doesn't cover the same criteria for why you may want to `skip` a test step.

I currently put `if` statements around specific steps which means there is no mention of it being skipped in reports.
If I mark it as `fixme` or `fail` it will report, but be incorrect.

From a DX perspective, having `only` is incredibly helpful.

Thanks :)

> From a DX perspective, having `only` is incredibly helpful.

Btw, what is your use-case for `step.only`? I assume running single step out of other steps will always fail due to missing context.
We run a lot of UI tests (not in an e2e journey), so isolating and running a specific test step would be helpful if a test is big

review_comments: So we do not consider timeout a valid "fail" situation? I guess that's similar to `test.fail()`? Perhaps mention it in the docs?
